en.title: Microbiology: the whole course
en.short: What microbiology covers, how microbiology degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What microbiology is
sections.text:
Microbiology is the study of organisms too small to see clearly with the naked eye: bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa and algae, and also viruses, which are not cells at all. It covers how they are built, how they grow, how they are identified, how they cause disease, and how people use them in food, industry, agriculture and waste treatment.

It matters for health, because infectious disease is still a leading cause of death in much of Africa, and for food and water safety and for biotechnology. It is also a laboratory science, learnt with your hands as much as from a book.

These notes teach principles and standard methods. They do not replace your laboratory manual, your department’s safety rules or your country’s regulations.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.

In Nigeria a BSc in microbiology usually takes four years, and many programmes include a supervised industrial attachment, often under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnics commonly offer an ND and then an HND in Science Laboratory Technology with a microbiology option. A Nigerian MSc usually takes one to two years.

In the UK a BSc usually takes three years, or four with a placement year; in Scotland usually four. A taught MSc normally takes one year full time. Ghana, Kenya and other countries have their own patterns.

Medical, veterinary and pharmacy students take microbiology as a service course. Medical graduates who specialise later train as medical microbiologists.

sections.heading: The first stage: foundations
sections.text:
The opening topics give you the tools.

History and scope explains how the field grew, from Leeuwenhoek’s microscopes through Pasteur and Koch to modern genomics. Microscopy and staining covers light and electron microscopy, the Gram stain and the acid-fast stain. Cell structure compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells: wall, membrane, ribosomes, chromosome, plasmids and flagella. Diversity and classification covers the three-domain system and how organisms are named.

Nutrition, growth and culture covers media, growth curves and generation time. Metabolism covers respiration and fermentation. Microbial genetics introduces DNA, mutation and gene transfer. Control of microorganisms covers sterilisation and disinfection. Laboratory methods and biosafety covers aseptic technique and biosafety levels. Quantitative methods gives the statistics you need to judge data.

sections.heading: The core and master’s stages
sections.text:
Core topics apply the foundations. Bacterial genetics covers transformation, transduction and conjugation. Immunology covers innate and adaptive immunity. Medical bacteriology, virology, mycology and parasitology cover the major pathogens and how they cause disease. Antimicrobial chemotherapy covers drug classes and resistance. Diagnostic microbiology covers specimens, culture and identification. Epidemiology and infection control covers how infections spread and how to stop them.

Applied topics follow: food, industrial and biotechnology, environmental, and agricultural and plant microbiology. Research methods, professional practice, ethics and biosafety close the core.

At master’s level come advanced genomics and bioinformatics, host-pathogen interactions, metabolic engineering, and a research project and dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the vocabulary exactly. A colony, a culture and a strain are not the same thing, and examiners notice.

Draw and label: a bacterial cell, a growth curve, a Gram stain result, an infection cycle. Drawing forces you to notice what you would otherwise skim.

Do the arithmetic. If a culture rises from 10³ to 10⁶ cells per millilitre in 3 hours, that is about 10 generations, because 2¹⁰ is about 1000. The generation time is 180 ÷ 10 = 18 minutes. Practise dilution and colony-count sums the same way, and check that answers are plausible.

Keep a laboratory notebook properly, including failed results. Read one short review per topic. Learn the safety rules before you enter the laboratory.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
The commonest mistake is confusing sterilisation with disinfection, or disinfection with antisepsis. Another is expecting antibiotics to act on viruses; they do not.

Students also mix up prokaryotic and eukaryotic features, misread Gram stains, forget controls, and record only the results they expected. In calculations the usual errors are dilution factors and converting colony counts to colony-forming units per millilitre.

Some memorise taxonomy and forget function. Names change as classification improves, so check a current source rather than an old handout.

Do not assume that one country’s biosafety rules, vaccine schedules or reporting requirements apply in another. Check current official guidance where you study.

keyPoints: Microbiology studies bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses, and how they grow, cause disease and are put to use.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
The course moves from microscopy, cell structure and growth to pathogens, immunology, control and the applied fields.
Sterilisation kills all microorganisms, disinfection reduces them on objects, and antisepsis applies to living tissue.
Antibiotics do not act on viruses, so they are useless against viral infections.
Do the calculations, draw and label diagrams, and keep an honest laboratory notebook.

en.title: History, scope and branches of microbiology
en.short: From van Leeuwenhoek to Pasteur, Koch and Winogradsky, plus germ theory, branches and importance.

sections.heading: First observations
sections.text:
Microbiology began when Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth merchant, used simple single-lens microscopes to see bacteria and protozoa in the 1670s. He called them animalcules and reported them to the Royal Society in London.

The old belief in spontaneous generation held that living things arise from non-living matter. Francesco Redi showed in 1668 that maggots come from fly eggs, not meat. Louis Pasteur settled the debate in 1861. In his swan-neck flask experiment, boiled broth in a flask with a curved neck stayed sterile because dust and microbes settled in the bend; when the neck was broken, the broth spoiled. This showed that microbes come from the air, not from the broth itself.

sections.heading: Germ theory and postulates
sections.text:
Pasteur’s work supported the germ theory of disease: specific microorganisms cause specific diseases. Robert Koch, a German physician, gave the theory a practical test. His postulates state that the organism must be found in all cases of the disease, be grown in pure culture, cause the same disease when inoculated into a healthy host, and be re-isolated from that host. Koch identified the causes of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera. The postulates still guide how scientists link microbes to disease, but they fail for organisms that cannot be cultured or that cause disease only in some hosts.

Sergei Winogradsky, a Russian microbiologist, showed that some bacteria obtain energy by oxidising inorganic compounds, a process called chemolithotrophy. He discovered nitrifying and sulfur bacteria and described nitrogen fixation. His work founded environmental and soil microbiology.

sections.heading: Branches and importance
sections.text:
Microbiology now covers bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses. Its branches include medical microbiology, agricultural and plant microbiology, industrial microbiology, food microbiology, environmental microbiology, immunology, virology and microbial genetics.

The importance is broad. In medicine, microbiology identifies pathogens and supports vaccines and antibiotics. In agriculture, it explains soil fertility, nitrogen fixation and plant disease. In industry, microbes make antibiotics, enzymes, foods and fuels. In the environment, they drive nutrient cycles and waste treatment.

keyPoints: Van Leeuwenhoek first saw microorganisms in the 1670s using simple microscopes.
Pasteur’s swan-neck flask experiments disproved spontaneous generation and supported the germ theory.
Koch’s postulates link a specific microorganism to a specific disease.
Winogradsky discovered chemolithotrophy and founded soil and environmental microbiology.
Microbiology has branches in medicine, agriculture, industry, food and the environment.
Microorganisms drive nutrient cycles and are used to make vaccines, antibiotics and foods.

en.title: Microscopy and staining
en.short: Light, fluorescence and electron microscopy, specimen preparation and key staining methods.

sections.heading: Light microscopy
sections.text: Magnification is how much larger an image appears; total magnification = objective × eyepiece. Resolution is the smallest distance at which two points are seen as separate. For a light microscope, d = 0.61 × λ ÷ NA, where λ is wavelength and numerical aperture (NA) = n sin θ. A higher NA or shorter wavelength gives better resolution. Immersion oil raises NA by matching refractive indices. Contrast is the difference in brightness or colour between specimen and background; stains increase it. Example: λ = 550 nm and NA = 1.25 give d = 0.61 × 550 ÷ 1.25 ≈ 268 nm.

sections.heading: Fluorescence and electron microscopy
sections.text: Fluorescence microscopy uses fluorophores: dyes that absorb light of one wavelength and emit light of a longer wavelength. Filters separate excitation from emission, so labelled structures glow against a dark background. Attaching dyes to antibodies lets molecules be shown. Electron microscopes use an electron beam and electromagnetic lenses. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) passes electrons through thin sections; scanning electron microscopy (SEM) scans surfaces. The electron wavelength is short, so resolution is far better than light microscopy, but specimens are fixed, dehydrated and viewed in a vacuum, so living cells cannot be examined.

sections.heading: Wet mounts and smears
sections.text: A wet mount is a drop of specimen in liquid covered by a coverslip. It keeps organisms alive, so motility can be seen. A smear is a thin film of specimen on a slide. It is air-dried and heat-fixed to attach cells to the slide before staining.

sections.heading: Stains
sections.text: Simple stains use one dye to show shape and arrangement. Differential stains separate groups. In Gram staining, crystal violet is applied, then iodine (a mordant, which fixes the dye in the cells), then alcohol decolouriser, then safranin. Gram-positive cells retain the purple crystal violet; Gram-negative cells lose it and take the pink counterstain. Acid-fast staining (Ziehl-Neelsen) uses carbol fuchsin with heat, acid-alcohol to decolourise, and methylene blue. Acid-fast cells stay red; others are blue. Special stains show capsules, endospores or flagella.

keyPoints: Total magnification = objective magnification × eyepiece magnification.
Resolution improves as numerical aperture rises and wavelength falls; d = 0.61 × λ ÷ NA.
Fluorescence uses excitation and emission light; electron microscopy gives higher resolution but needs fixed specimens.
Wet mounts keep organisms alive; smears are dried and heat-fixed before staining.
Gram staining gives Gram-positive cells purple and Gram-negative cells pink or red.
Acid-fast staining keeps acid-fast cells red and colours others blue.

en.title: Microbial cell structure and function
en.short: Covers prokaryote and eukaryote cells, bacterial envelope, appendages, endospores, and archaea, fungi and protozoa.

sections.heading: Prokaryote and eukaryote
sections.text: Prokaryotic microbial cells, the bacteria and archaea, lack a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles. Their DNA lies in a nucleoid, and their ribosomes are 70S. Eukaryotic microbial cells, such as fungi and protozoa, have a nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum and 80S ribosomes; some also have cell walls. Eukaryotic cells are usually larger and more compartmentalised. This difference in organisation affects cell size, division and the action of antimicrobial drugs.

sections.heading: Bacterial envelope and appendages
sections.text: The bacterial envelope is the cytoplasmic membrane plus the cell wall, and in Gram-negative bacteria an outer membrane. The cytoplasmic membrane is a phospholipid bilayer that controls entry and exit and carries respiratory enzymes. The wall gives shape and prevents lysis; peptidoglycan is a sugar polymer cross-linked by short peptides. The outer membrane contains lipopolysaccharide in many Gram-negative bacteria. A capsule is a layer outside the wall that protects the cell and aids adherence. Flagella are long appendages for motility. Pili are shorter hairs for attachment and, in conjugation, DNA transfer. Endospores are dormant, heat-resistant forms made by genera such as Bacillus and Clostridium; they are not reproductive. Not all bacteria have capsules or flagella. In a soil sample, Bacillus may swim by flagella and form endospores when nutrients run low.

sections.heading: Archaea, fungi and protozoa
sections.text: Archaea resemble bacteria in shape but differ in chemistry: their membranes use ether-linked lipids, and their walls lack peptidoglycan, though some have pseudopeptidoglycan. Fungi are eukaryotic, with chitin walls and ergosterol in their membranes; they grow as hyphae or yeasts. Fungal walls may also contain other polysaccharides. Protozoa are eukaryotic and usually lack a cell wall; they move by cilia, flagella or pseudopodia. In a pond water sample, a ciliated protozoan, a yeast and a bacterium can be separated by these features.

keyPoints: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotes have one.
Peptidoglycan is the main bacterial wall polymer; Gram-negative walls also have an outer membrane.
Capsules, flagella and pili lie outside the wall and serve protection, motility and attachment.
Endospores are dormant resistant forms, not a means of reproduction.
Archaea differ in membrane lipids and wall chemistry; fungi have chitin walls; protozoa usually lack walls.
The cytoplasmic membrane controls transport and houses respiratory enzymes.

en.title: Microbial diversity and classification
en.short: Survey of microbial groups, taxonomy, three domains and identification methods.

sections.heading: Major groups
sections.text: Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes: cells without a membrane-bound nucleus. Most bacteria have peptidoglycan in the cell wall; archaea lack peptidoglycan and have different membrane lipids. Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs with chitinous walls, growing as yeasts or moulds. Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotic heterotrophs, often motile. Algae are photosynthetic eukaryotes, mostly aquatic. Viruses are not cells: they have nucleic acid inside a protein capsid, sometimes an envelope, and reproduce only inside a host cell.

sections.heading: Taxonomy and naming
sections.text: Taxonomy is the science of describing, classifying and naming organisms. Classification groups organisms by shared features; nomenclature gives names. The main ranks are domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Binomial nomenclature uses two names: genus with a capital letter and species in lower case, both italicised in print. For example, Escherichia coli is a bacterium; the genus is Escherichia, the species epithet coli. Names are governed by codes that differ for bacteria, fungi, algae, protozoa and viruses.

sections.heading: Three domains
sections.text: The three-domain system places cellular life in Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. It rests mainly on ribosomal RNA sequence comparisons, especially small-subunit rRNA. Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotic domains; Eukarya includes fungi, protozoa and algae. Viruses are outside this system because they are not cellular and are classified separately by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses. A case: a water sample from a well in Kaduna grows a tiny colony. Microscopy shows no nucleus, and gene sequencing places it in Archaea, not Bacteria.

sections.heading: Identification methods
sections.text: Major groups are identified by a combination of methods. Microscopy and staining show shape, size and cell-wall type. Culture on selective media and biochemical tests reveal growth needs and metabolism. Serology uses antibodies. Molecular methods are now central: 16S rRNA gene sequencing for bacteria and archaea, ITS (internal transcribed spacer) regions for fungi, and PCR or whole-genome sequencing for many groups. MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry is used in many diagnostic laboratories. No single test is enough; identification combines several results.

keyPoints: Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes; fungi, protozoa and algae are eukaryotes; viruses are acellular.
The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, based largely on rRNA sequence comparisons.
Binomial nomenclature gives each species a genus name and a species epithet, both italicised in print.
Viruses are classified separately from cellular life, by the ICTV.
Identification combines microscopy, culture, biochemical tests, serology and molecular methods.
16S rRNA gene sequencing is a standard method for identifying bacteria and archaea.

en.title: Microbial nutrition, growth and culture
en.short: Nutrient needs, transport, media, pure culture, growth curve, generation time and conditions.

sections.heading: Nutrition and transport
sections.text: Microbes need a carbon source, an energy source, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulphur, trace metals and water. Autotrophs use carbon dioxide; heterotrophs use organic carbon. Transport across the membrane may be passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion through proteins, active transport using energy, or group translocation, where the substance is changed as it enters. Iron is often captured by siderophores.

sections.heading: Media and pure culture
sections.text: A culture medium supplies these nutrients. Defined media have known ingredients; complex media use digests such as peptone. Selective media favour one group and inhibit others; differential media show a visible difference, such as colour. Solid media contain agar, a gelling agent. To isolate bacteria, streak a plate, spread a dilution or pour a sample in agar. A pure culture comes from one colony and contains one organism.

sections.heading: Growth curve and generation time
sections.text: In batch culture, nutrients are not replaced. Numbers pass through lag, exponential (log), stationary and death phases. During exponential growth, Nt = N0 × 2^n, where n is the number of divisions. Generation time g = t ÷ n. Example: a culture rises from 1.0 × 10^5 to 8.0 × 10^5 cells in 90 min. This is an 8-fold rise, so n = 3 because 2³ = 8. Then g = 90 ÷ 3 = 30 min. Continuous culture, such as a chemostat, adds fresh medium and removes culture, keeping growth near a chosen rate.

sections.heading: Environment and culture systems
sections.text: Temperature, pH, water activity and oxygen control growth. Each organism has minimum, optimum and maximum temperatures; some are cold-loving psychrophiles, moderate mesophiles or heat-loving thermophiles. Most bacteria grow best near pH 6.5 to 7.5, though some prefer acid or alkaline conditions. Water activity (aw) measures available water; drying or adding salt lowers it. Oxygen categories include obligate aerobes, which need oxygen; facultative anaerobes, which can grow with or without it; microaerophiles, which need low oxygen; and obligate anaerobes, which cannot tolerate it.

keyPoints: Nutrients supply carbon, energy, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulphur, trace metals and water.
Transport may be passive, facilitated, active or group translocation.
Defined, selective and differential media help isolation; a pure culture comes from one colony.
Batch growth has lag, exponential, stationary and death phases; Nt = N0 × 2^n and g = t ÷ n.
Continuous culture adds fresh medium and removes culture to hold growth near a chosen rate.
Temperature, pH, water activity and oxygen determine which organisms grow.

en.title: Microbial metabolism
en.short: Enzymes, energy conservation, respiration, fermentation, photosynthesis, chemolithotrophy and ATP yield.

sections.heading: Enzymes and energy
sections.text:
Metabolism is all the chemical reactions in a cell. Catabolic pathways break molecules down and release energy; anabolic pathways build molecules and use energy. Enzymes are protein catalysts that speed reactions by lowering activation energy, the energy needed to start a reaction. They do not change the equilibrium.

Energy released in catabolism is conserved as ATP, the cell’s energy currency, and as reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH2. ATP is made by substrate-level phosphorylation, when a phosphate is transferred from a substrate to ADP, or by chemiosmosis, when a proton gradient drives ATP synthase.

sections.heading: Respiration and fermentation
sections.text:
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor. Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate, then the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain oxidise it completely. Anaerobic respiration uses the same general route but a different final acceptor, such as nitrate or sulphate, so it yields less ATP.

Fermentation does not use an electron transport chain. It regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue, and the organic product, such as lactate or ethanol, is excreted. Fermentation yields only the 2 ATP net of glycolysis.

sections.heading: Photosynthesis and chemolithotrophy
sections.text: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make ATP and NADPH, then fixes CO2 into organic matter. Oxygenic phototrophs use water as electron donor and release oxygen; anoxygenic phototrophs use other donors. Chemolithotrophy is the oxidation of inorganic compounds such as ammonia, hydrogen sulphide or ferrous iron to conserve energy. Many chemolithotrophs fix CO2 and so are autotrophs.

sections.heading: Pathways and ATP yield
sections.text:
Catabolism supplies ATP, NADH, FADH2 and carbon skeletons; anabolism uses them to build cell material. ATP yield is theoretical and varies with the organism and the electron acceptor. For glucose, glycolysis gives 2 ATP and 2 NADH; pyruvate oxidation gives 2 NADH; the Krebs cycle gives 2 ATP, 6 NADH and 2 FADH2.

Using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2:
2 + (2×2.5) + (2×2.5) + 2 + (6×2.5) + (2×1.5) = 32 ATP
Older texts use 3 and 2 and give 38. Check your course’s convention.

keyPoints: Enzymes lower activation energy but do not change the equilibrium or the overall free-energy change.
Catabolism releases energy and anabolism uses it; ATP and NADH or FADH2 couple the two.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen as final electron acceptor and yields the most ATP.
Anaerobic respiration uses other final electron acceptors and yields less ATP than aerobic respiration.
Fermentation regenerates NAD+ and yields only the 2 ATP net of glycolysis.
For glucose, using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2 gives 32 ATP; the older 3 and 2 convention gives 38.

en.title: Introduction to microbial genetics
en.short: DNA, replication, transcription, translation, mutation, repair, plasmids, recombination and gene regulation in microbes.

sections.heading: DNA and replication
sections.text: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands. Each nucleotide has a sugar, phosphate and base: A, T, G or C. Hydrogen bonds join A to T and G to C. Bacterial chromosomes are usually circular, though some are linear. Replication is semi-conservative: each strand templates a new strand. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only 5′ to 3′, so the leading strand is continuous and the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments. Primase makes primers, helicase unwinds, and ligase seals nicks.

sections.heading: From gene to protein
sections.text: Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template. RNA polymerase binds a promoter, unwinds DNA and builds RNA 5′ to 3′, using U in place of T. In bacteria, translation can begin before transcription ends. Translation uses ribosomes, tRNA and mRNA. Each codon of three bases specifies an amino acid; AUG is usually the start codon and UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. The code is degenerate: several codons can specify one amino acid.

sections.heading: Mutation and repair
sections.text: A mutation is a heritable change in DNA sequence. A point mutation substitutes one base. An insertion or deletion can shift the reading frame. Mutations may be silent, missense (a different amino acid) or nonsense (a stop codon). Repair includes proofreading by DNA polymerase, mismatch repair and excision repair. Example: a base change in the rpoB gene can alter RNA polymerase so rifampicin no longer binds; this is a common route to rifampicin resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

sections.heading: Plasmids, recombination and regulation
sections.text: Plasmids are small extrachromosomal DNA molecules that replicate independently; they may carry genes such as antibiotic resistance. Recombination exchanges DNA between similar sequences (homologous recombination) or at specific sites (site-specific recombination). Gene regulation lets cells respond to conditions. An operon is a set of genes controlled together. In the lac operon of E. coli, the repressor blocks transcription when lactose is absent. When lactose is present it binds the repressor, and if glucose is low, CAP-cAMP activates transcription. Lactose is used only when needed.

keyPoints: DNA is a double helix; A pairs with T and G with C, and replication is semi-conservative.
DNA polymerase builds DNA 5′ to 3′, so the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments.
Transcription makes RNA from DNA; translation uses mRNA codons, ribosomes and tRNA to make protein.
Mutations are heritable DNA changes; repair systems correct many errors, but some changes persist.
Plasmids are extrachromosomal DNA molecules that can carry useful or resistance genes.
The lac operon shows gene regulation: lactose and glucose levels control transcription.

en.title: Control of microorganisms
en.short: Sterilisation, disinfection, antisepsis and preservation; physical and chemical methods, resistance and testing.

sections.heading: Terms and targets
sections.text: Control means killing microorganisms or stopping their growth. Sterilisation destroys or removes all microbial life, including bacterial endospores. Disinfection reduces pathogens on inanimate surfaces but may leave spores. Antisepsis is disinfection applied to skin or living tissue. Preservation stops spoilage organisms growing in a product. A microbicidal agent kills; a microbistatic agent only inhibits growth, and growth may resume when it is removed.

sections.heading: Physical methods
sections.text: Heat is the most reliable physical method. Moist heat under pressure, as in an autoclave, coagulates proteins and kills spores; dry heat oxidises cell components. Filtration removes microbes from liquids and air. Radiation damages nucleic acids: ultraviolet light is used for surfaces and air, ionising radiation for heat-sensitive supplies. The choice depends on the item. A glass bottle may be autoclaved, but a heat-sensitive vaccine is filtered.

sections.heading: Chemical agents
sections.text: Chemical agents include alcohols, phenolics, halogens, oxidising agents, aldehydes and quaternary ammonium compounds. They act by denaturing proteins, disrupting membranes or damaging nucleic acids. Preservatives are chemical agents that inhibit growth in products. Resistance is common: spores and biofilms shield cells, organic matter inactivates some agents, and some bacteria carry efflux pumps that expel chemicals from the cell. Always use the correct concentration and contact time. Case: a spilled culture is covered with disinfectant, left for the stated contact time, then cleaned; wiping first without disinfectant spreads contamination.

sections.heading: Testing and chemotherapy
sections.text: Disinfectants are tested by suspension tests, surface tests and in-use tests. The old phenol coefficient compares an agent with phenol, but modern standards measure log reduction, a tenfold drop in surviving cells, under defined conditions. Antimicrobial chemotherapy is different: it uses drugs that are selectively toxic to the pathogen inside the body. This summary only introduces the concept; the drugs themselves belong to a later topic.

keyPoints: Sterilisation kills or removes all microbes including endospores; disinfection, antisepsis and preservation have narrower aims.
Moist heat in an autoclave is the most reliable method; filtration and radiation suit heat-sensitive items.
Chemical agents act by denaturing proteins, disrupting membranes or damaging nucleic acids.
Spores, biofilms, organic matter and efflux pumps can make microbes resistant to control agents.
Disinfectants are tested by suspension, surface and in-use tests, and modern tests measure log reduction.
Antimicrobial chemotherapy uses selectively toxic drugs inside the body; it is introduced here only as a concept.

en.title: Laboratory methods and biosafety
en.short: Aseptic technique, media, pure cultures, biosafety levels, waste disposal and laboratory records.

sections.heading: Aseptic technique
sections.text: Aseptic technique means working so that unwanted microbes do not enter cultures, surfaces or the worker. Flame a loop until red hot, let it cool near the flame, and work close to a Bunsen flame or inside a biological safety cabinet when the risk requires it. Hold tube caps in the little finger, never put them down. Do not touch sterile surfaces.

sections.heading: Media and pure cultures
sections.text: Media are nutrient preparations that support growth. Weigh ingredients as the label says, dissolve, adjust pH if required, then sterilise. Most media are autoclaved; heat-labile liquids are filter-sterilised. Cool molten agar to about 50 °C before pouring plates. Inoculation is the transfer of microbes into or onto medium. Isolation uses streak, spread or pour plates to separate cells so that a single colony can be picked. A pure culture contains one organism. Maintain it by transferring it to fresh agar slants or by storing a labelled stock as the laboratory specifies.

sections.heading: Biosafety and waste
sections.text: Biosafety levels (BSL-1 to BSL-4) describe containment for increasing hazard. BSL-1 covers low-risk work; BSL-2 adds restricted access, personal protective equipment (PPE) and a biosafety cabinet for splashes; BSL-3 and BSL-4 are for serious pathogens and need specialist facilities. Follow the WHO Laboratory Biosafety Manual and your country’s rules. Containment combines facility, equipment and safe practice. Autoclave contaminated cultures and plates before disposal. Put sharps in a sharps container. Clean spills with disinfectant, report incidents, wash hands, and never eat or drink in the laboratory.

sections.heading: Records and quality
sections.text: Record the date, medium batch, organism, method, incubation conditions and observations in a notebook. Label every plate and tube. Quality checks include sterility checks, growth-promotion tests for media, equipment calibration and written procedures. Case: Ada streaks a plate, labels it, incubates it inverted and records the result. A colony growing outside the streak line means the plate is not pure; she does not use it as a stock culture.

keyPoints: Aseptic technique keeps unwanted microbes out of cultures and away from the worker.
Media must be prepared as labelled and sterilised before use; heat-labile liquids are filter-sterilised.
Inoculation transfers microbes to medium, and isolation separates them until a single colony can be picked.
A pure culture contains one organism and is maintained by fresh subculture or a labelled stock.
Biosafety levels BSL-1 to BSL-4 describe increasing containment; follow WHO and national rules.
Record every batch and result, and autoclave contaminated waste before disposal.

en.title: Quantitative methods and biostatistics for microbiology
en.short: Units, dilution and viable counts, MPN, descriptive statistics, graphs and simple tests.

sections.heading: Units and dilution
sections.text:
Microbiologists measure volume in millilitres (mL) or microlitres (µL), mass in grams, and concentration in colony forming units per mL (CFU/mL). A serial dilution multiplies dilution factors. Adding 1 mL of sample to 9 mL diluent gives a 10-fold dilution, factor 10⁻¹; repeating it gives 10⁻², and so on.

Example: plate 0.1 mL of a 10⁻⁵ dilution and count 50 colonies.
CFU/mL = colonies ÷ (volume plated × dilution)
= 50 ÷ (0.1 × 10⁻⁵) = 5.0 × 10⁷ CFU/mL
Use a countable plate, often about 30 to 300 colonies; labs set their own range.

sections.heading: Viable counts and MPN
sections.text: A viable count assumes each colony grows from one living cell or clump, so it counts CFU, not individual cells. Spread plates and pour plates are common. The most probable number (MPN) method uses replicate liquid cultures at several dilutions. You record which tubes show growth and read the MPN from a published table for that tube design. MPN is a statistical estimate with a confidence interval, not an exact count.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise data. The mean is the sum divided by n; the median is the middle value; the mode is the most frequent. Standard deviation (s) measures spread. The standard error of the mean, s ÷ √n, estimates sampling error: how much a sample mean may differ from the population mean.

Choose graphs to suit data: bar charts for categories, histograms for continuous measurements, scatter plots for relationships, and line graphs for change over time. Label axes and units.

sections.heading: Simple tests
sections.text: A hypothesis test compares observed data with a null hypothesis. The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme if the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the null is true. A t-test compares two means, and a chi-square test compares observed and expected counts. Report the test, the statistic, the degrees of freedom and the p-value, and give a confidence interval where possible.

keyPoints: Dilution factor multiplies at each step: 1 mL into 9 mL gives 10⁻¹.
CFU/mL = colonies ÷ (volume plated in mL × dilution).
MPN is read from tables for the tube design and is an estimate with a confidence interval.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; standard deviation s measures spread; standard error of the mean = s ÷ √n.
Use bar charts for categories, histograms for continuous data and scatter plots for relationships.
A t-test compares two means and a chi-square test compares counts; p is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

en.title: Bacterial genetics and gene transfer
en.short: Bacterial genome organisation, mutation and repair, and gene transfer by transformation, conjugation and transduction.

sections.heading: Genome and mutation
sections.text:
Most bacteria have one circular chromosome, a single copy of each gene and no nucleus. The DNA is coiled in the nucleoid. Many also carry plasmids, small extrachromosomal DNA molecules that replicate independently. Genes are often grouped in operons, so one promoter controls several genes. The chromosome plus plasmids form the genome.

Mutation is a change in DNA sequence. A point mutation replaces one base; insertions or deletions can shift the reading frame. Mutations may be silent, missense or nonsense. Repair includes proofreading by DNA polymerase, mismatch repair, excision repair and the SOS response. Most mutations are neutral or harmful.

sections.heading: Gene transfer
sections.text: Transformation is uptake of naked DNA from environment. A competent cell binds DNA, takes it in and may integrate it into its chromosome by recombination. Conjugation needs contact between cells. A conjugative plasmid carries genes for a sex pilus and a mating bridge; one strand of plasmid DNA passes into the recipient, which makes the second strand. F plasmid of Escherichia coli is a classic example. Transduction is gene transfer by bacteriophages. In generalised transduction, a phage accidentally packages host DNA instead of its own and injects it into another bacterium. In specialised transduction, a temperate phage carries a few host genes next to its integration site.

sections.heading: Mobile DNA and resistance
sections.text:
Plasmids are extrachromosomal replicons; resistance plasmids carry antibiotic resistance genes. Transposons are DNA segments that move within or between genomes. Insertion sequences are simple transposons; composite transposons carry extra genes between two insertion sequences. Integrons are gene capture systems: an integrase inserts gene cassettes at a specific site, and a promoter expresses them.

Case: a patient in Lagos, Nigeria, with a wound infection has Klebsiella pneumoniae carrying a plasmid with an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) gene. The plasmid can pass by conjugation to another Klebsiella or E. coli. The gene may sit in a transposon or integron. Such transfer spreads resistance and aids adaptation.

keyPoints: Most bacteria have one circular chromosome, a single copy of each gene and no nucleus, and many also carry plasmids.
Mutation changes DNA sequence; repair systems include proofreading, mismatch repair, excision repair and the SOS response.
Transformation takes up naked DNA, conjugation transfers DNA through cell contact, and transduction uses bacteriophages.
Plasmids replicate independently, transposons move DNA segments, and integrons capture and express gene cassettes.
Horizontal gene transfer spreads antibiotic resistance genes and helps bacteria adapt to new environments.
A resistance plasmid can pass by conjugation from Klebsiella pneumoniae to E. coli, for example.

en.title: Immunology: innate and adaptive immunity
en.short: Innate and adaptive immunity, antigens, antibodies, complement, T and B cells, vaccines and memory.

sections.heading: Innate immunity
sections.text: Innate immunity is the first line. It is fast, broad and has no memory. Barriers such as skin and mucus stop microbes. Phagocytes, mainly neutrophils and macrophages, recognise common microbial patterns and ingest microbes. Complement is a group of plasma proteins that coat microbes, attract phagocytes and can puncture microbial membranes. Inflammation brings more cells and fluid to the site. These responses limit infection but do not target one antigen precisely.

sections.heading: Adaptive immunity
sections.text: Adaptive immunity is slower at first and highly specific. An antigen is any molecule that a lymphocyte receptor or antibody recognises. B cells make antibodies; T cells help other cells or kill infected cells. Helper T cells activate B cells and macrophages, while cytotoxic T cells destroy infected cells. After an infection, some B and T cells become memory cells. A later encounter with the same antigen triggers a faster, stronger response.

sections.heading: Antibodies and complement
sections.text: An antibody is a Y-shaped immunoglobulin made by plasma cells, which are activated B cells. Antibodies bind antigens and may neutralise toxins or viruses, block attachment, or mark microbes for phagocytes and complement. Complement can also form pores in bacterial membranes. Antibody and complement therefore work together, linking specific recognition to destruction.

sections.heading: Active, passive and vaccines
sections.text: Active immunity develops when the body makes its own response, after infection or vaccination. Passive immunity is borrowed: ready-made antibodies pass from mother to baby or are given in antibody preparations, giving quick but temporary protection. Vaccines present antigens safely, often as weakened or killed pathogens or inactivated toxins, so the immune system forms memory without severe disease. Example: Amina receives a measles vaccine. Her immune system makes antibody and memory cells. Years later, measles virus exposure is controlled quickly because memory cells respond before illness develops.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast, broad and lacks memory; phagocytes and complement are central.
Adaptive immunity is specific and has memory, carried out by B and T lymphocytes.
Antigens are recognised by lymphocyte receptors and antibodies; antibodies are made by plasma cells.
Helper T cells coordinate responses and cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells.
Active immunity follows infection or vaccination; passive immunity gives ready-made antibodies and is temporary.
Vaccines create immunological memory, so later exposure is controlled faster and more strongly.

en.title: Medical bacteriology: bacterial pathogenesis and major pathogens
en.short: How bacteria cause disease, from adhesion and toxins to major pathogens and their infections.

sections.heading: Pathogenesis stages
sections.text: Pathogenesis is the chain from exposure to disease. A pathogen must reach a susceptible site, adhere, multiply, often invade or release toxins, and evade host defences. Virulence factors are bacterial molecules or structures that promote these steps. Colonisation means stable growth at a body surface without necessarily causing disease. Whether disease follows depends on dose, route, strain and host immunity. A student in Kano with fever, neck stiffness and small bleeding spots suggests meningococcal meningitis; laboratory confirmation is needed.

sections.heading: Adhesion and invasion
sections.text: Adhesion uses pili (fimbriae), capsules and surface proteins to bind host cells. Escherichia coli that causes diarrhoea may attach by fimbriae to intestinal cells. Invasion is entry into host cells or tissues, helped by invasins (entry proteins) and secretion systems that inject bacterial proteins. Some bacteria remain extracellular; others, such as Listeria monocytogenes, enter cells and spread. Invasion can breach barriers and carry bacteria into the blood, causing bacteraemia. Not every invasion causes disease.

sections.heading: Toxins and immune evasion
sections.text: Exotoxins are proteins secreted by bacteria. They include two-part A-B toxins, which bind a cell and deliver an active subunit; cytolytic toxins that damage membranes; and superantigens that overstimulate T cells. Endotoxin is lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane of Gram-negative (pink-staining) bacteria; it triggers fever and shock when released. Immune evasion includes capsules that resist phagocytosis (engulfing by white cells), IgA protease, protein A (which binds antibodies), antigenic variation and survival inside phagocytes. Such factors help infections persist or recur.

sections.heading: Major pathogens
sections.text: Major Gram-positive (purple-staining) pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus (skin, wound and blood infections), Streptococcus pyogenes (pharyngitis, impetigo, rheumatic fever), Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumonia, meningitis), Corynebacterium diphtheriae (diphtheria) and Clostridium tetani (tetanus). Mycobacterium tuberculosis (tuberculosis) is acid-fast (retains stain after acid wash). Gram-negative examples are Neisseria meningitidis (meningitis), Escherichia coli (diarrhoea, urinary infection), Salmonella Typhi (typhoid), Shigella (dysentery), Vibrio cholerae (cholera), Helicobacter pylori (ulcers) and Bordetella pertussis (whooping cough). Spirochaetes (spiral bacteria) include Treponema pallidum (syphilis). This list is selective.

keyPoints: Pathogenesis requires adhesion, multiplication, often invasion or toxin production, and immune evasion.
Virulence factors are bacterial structures or molecules that promote infection.
Exotoxins are secreted proteins; endotoxin is Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide.
Capsules, IgA protease and antigenic variation help bacteria evade host immunity.

Major pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Neisseria meningitidis, Escherichia coli, Salmonella Typhi, Shigella and Vibrio cholerae.
Laboratory confirmation is needed for suspected bacterial infections.

en.title: Virology: viruses, replication and antiviral principles
en.short: Virus structure, classification, replication, cultivation, pathogenesis, major infections and antiviral principles.

sections.heading: Structure and classification
sections.text:
Viruses are small infectious agents with a DNA or RNA genome inside a protein capsid. Some have a lipid envelope with glycoproteins. Enveloped viruses are fragile and killed by soap and alcohol; non-enveloped viruses resist drying better.

Classification uses host, genome type (single- or double-stranded, positive or negative sense), morphology and replication strategy. The Baltimore system groups viruses into seven classes by how the genome is copied into messenger RNA. Influenza A is negative-sense RNA; HIV is positive-sense RNA; herpesviruses are double-stranded DNA.

sections.heading: Replication and assay
sections.text:
Replication follows attachment to a host receptor, entry, uncoating, genome replication and gene expression, assembly, and release. Enveloped viruses often bud through the membrane; non-enveloped viruses often lyse the cell. DNA viruses usually replicate in the nucleus, except poxviruses; RNA viruses usually replicate in the cytoplasm, except influenza. Retroviruses make DNA from RNA using reverse transcriptase.

Cultivation uses cell culture, eggs or animals; cytopathic effect is visible cell damage. Plaque assay counts infectious particles as plaque-forming units (PFU). Example: 0.1 mL of a 10^-4 dilution gives 40 plaques. PFU/mL = 40 ÷ (0.1 × 10^-4) = 4 × 10^6 PFU/mL.

sections.heading: Pathogenesis and transmission
sections.text:
Pathogenesis begins with entry, primary replication, spread and tropism, the range of cells a virus can infect. Damage comes from cell death and from the immune response. Transmission routes include respiratory droplets, faecal-oral, blood, sexual contact, vectors and mother to child.

Case: Aminu, a young child in Kano, has fever, cough and a rash. Measles spreads by droplets before the rash appears, so isolation and vaccinating contacts are important.

sections.heading: Infections and antivirals
sections.text:
Major viral infections include influenza, measles, poliomyelitis, HIV, hepatitis B and C, herpes, HPV, Ebola and SARS-CoV-2. Diagnosis uses PCR, antigen tests or serology.

Antivirals target specific steps: entry, uncoating, viral polymerase, protease, integrase or release. Examples are oseltamivir for influenza, tenofovir for HIV and hepatitis B, and sofosbuvir for hepatitis C. They do not replace vaccines. Antibiotics do not treat viruses. Resistance arises by mutation, so combination therapy is used.

keyPoints: Viruses have a DNA or RNA genome in a capsid; some have a lipid envelope.
Baltimore classification groups viruses by genome type and replication strategy.
Replication runs attachment, entry, uncoating, replication and expression, assembly, release.
Plaque assay: PFU/mL = plaque count ÷ (volume plated × dilution).
Transmission routes include droplets, faecal-oral, blood, sexual, vectors and mother to child.
Antivirals target viral steps; antibiotics do not treat viruses and vaccines prevent infection.

en.title: Mycology: fungi, mycoses and antifungal agents
en.short: Fungal biology, yeasts and moulds, mycoses, mycotoxins and antifungal drugs.

sections.heading: Fungal biology
sections.text:
Fungi are eukaryotes. Their cell walls contain chitin, not peptidoglycan, and their membranes contain ergosterol. They are heterotrophs: they secrete enzymes and absorb nutrients. Yeasts are unicellular and reproduce by budding. Moulds grow as branching threads called hyphae; a mass of hyphae is a mycelium. Some dimorphic fungi, such as Histoplasma capsulatum, grow as moulds in cool conditions and as yeasts in the host.

Classification uses morphology and molecular phylogeny. Standard texts recognise phyla such as Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, Mucoromycota and Chytridiomycota, but details change with new sequence data.

sections.heading: Mycoses
sections.text:
Mycosis means fungal infection. Superficial mycoses affect skin, hair or nails; dermatophytes cause tinea, commonly called ringworm, and Malassezia causes pityriasis versicolor. Subcutaneous mycoses enter through breaks in the skin. Sporothrix schenckii, for example, can follow a thorn prick and cause nodules along lymph vessels. Systemic mycoses affect deep tissues. They may follow inhalation or occur when immunity is low; examples include aspergillosis, cryptococcosis and invasive candidiasis.

Case: a gardener pricks a finger on a thorn. A painless ulcer and nodules appear up the arm. Culture grows Sporothrix schenckii. This is lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis.

sections.heading: Mycotoxins and drugs
sections.text:
Mycotoxins are toxic secondary metabolites produced by moulds in food or feed. Aflatoxin B1, from Aspergillus flavus, is a liver carcinogen; good drying and storage reduce risk. Other examples include ochratoxin A and fumonisins.

Antifungals exploit fungal targets. Polyenes such as amphotericin B bind ergosterol and damage the membrane. Azoles block ergosterol synthesis; terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase. Echinocandins inhibit β-1,3-glucan synthase. Flucytosine is converted inside fungi to a toxic metabolite. Because fungi are eukaryotes, many drugs are toxic to the patient, and resistance can develop.

keyPoints: Fungi are eukaryotes with chitin cell walls and ergosterol membranes.
Yeasts are unicellular; moulds form hyphae and mycelium; dimorphic fungi switch form.
Superficial mycoses affect skin, hair or nails; subcutaneous mycoses enter through skin; systemic mycoses affect deep tissues.
Aflatoxin B1 from Aspergillus flavus is a liver carcinogen; dry storage reduces risk.
Antifungals target ergosterol, ergosterol synthesis, β-1,3-glucan synthase or nucleic acid synthesis.
Fungi are eukaryotes, so antifungal toxicity and resistance are important.

en.title: Parasitology: protozoa and helminths
en.short: Protozoan and helminth life cycles, disease and diagnosis, with malaria and intestinal worms.

sections.heading: Parasite basics
sections.text:
Parasites live on or in a host. Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes; helminths are multicellular worms. A definitive host harbours the adult or sexual stage, an intermediate host harbours a larval or asexual stage, and a vector transmits the parasite between hosts.

Transmission routes include mosquito or fly bites, faecal-oral spread, and skin penetration by larvae. Diagnosis often uses microscopy of blood, stool or urine, plus antigen detection and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A case: a student in Ibadan with fever and anaemia has malaria tests by blood film and rapid antigen test.

sections.heading: Malaria and trypanosomiasis
sections.text:
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species and spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Sporozoites enter liver cells, then merozoites invade red cells; cycles of invasion and rupture cause fever. Haemolysis causes anaemia, and cytoadherence (infected red cells sticking to blood vessel walls) can lead to severe disease, including cerebral malaria. Diagnosis is by thick and thin blood films or rapid antigen tests.

African trypanosomiasis is caused by Trypanosoma brucei and spread by tsetse flies. It causes fever, swollen lymph nodes, later sleep disturbance and brain inflammation. American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease), caused by T. cruzi and spread by triatomine bugs, can damage the heart and gut. Diagnosis uses blood smears, antibody tests or PCR; in African trypanosomiasis, cerebrospinal fluid examination is used to stage late disease, while chronic Chagas disease is diagnosed by antibody tests.

sections.heading: Amoebiasis
sections.text:
Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan spread by faecal-oral transmission of cysts. Excystation (escape from the cyst) in the intestine releases trophozoites (feeding forms), which may invade the colon and cause dysentery or spread to the liver as an abscess.

Stool microscopy shows cysts or trophozoites, but antigen tests and PCR separate E. histolytica from the harmless E. dispar.

sections.heading: Intestinal helminths
sections.text:
Intestinal helminths include Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura and hookworms. Eggs passed in stool mature in soil; people ingest them or larvae penetrate skin. Adult worms cause malnutrition, anaemia, abdominal pain or obstruction.

Diagnosis is by stool microscopy for eggs or larvae. A child with iron-deficiency anaemia and hookworm eggs on stool microscopy shows the link between worm burden and blood loss.

keyPoints: Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes; helminths are multicellular worms.
Malaria is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes and diagnosed by blood films or rapid antigen tests.
African trypanosomiasis is spread by tsetse flies; American trypanosomiasis by triatomine bugs.
Entamoeba histolytica causes dysentery and liver abscess and must be distinguished from E. dispar.
Intestinal helminths are diagnosed by stool microscopy for eggs or larvae.
Prevention depends on vector control, safe water and sanitation, and hygiene.

en.title: Antimicrobial chemotherapy and resistance
en.short: Classes, mechanisms, selective toxicity, susceptibility testing, resistance and stewardship.

sections.heading: Selective toxicity
sections.text: Antimicrobial chemotherapy uses drugs to kill or stop microbes inside the body. Selective toxicity means harming the microbe more than the host. It relies on targets the host lacks or differs from: bacterial peptidoglycan cell wall, bacterial 70S ribosomes, fungal ergosterol, and viral enzymes. A drug with a narrow therapeutic index is risky because the useful dose is close to the toxic dose. Bactericidal drugs kill; bacteriostatic drugs stop growth and depend partly on host immunity.

sections.heading: Antibacterial agents
sections.text: Antibacterials act on a few main targets. Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams) and glycopeptides such as vancomycin inhibit cell wall synthesis. Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines bind the 30S ribosomal subunit; macrolides, clindamycin and chloramphenicol bind the 50S subunit. Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase or topoisomerase IV; rifamycins inhibit RNA polymerase. Sulfonamides and trimethoprim block folate synthesis. Metronidazole damages DNA in anaerobes. Because these targets are absent or different in human cells, selectivity is possible.

sections.heading: Antifungal and antiviral agents
sections.text: Antifungals exploit fungal features. Polyenes such as amphotericin B bind ergosterol and form pores. Azoles inhibit a cytochrome P450 enzyme in ergosterol synthesis. Echinocandins inhibit beta-1,3-glucan synthase, which builds the fungal cell wall. Flucytosine is converted to a toxic pyrimidine analogue inside fungal cells. Antivirals target viral proteins because viruses use host cells. Examples include acyclovir, a guanosine analogue activated by viral thymidine kinase to inhibit herpes DNA polymerase; oseltamivir, which inhibits influenza neuraminidase; and HIV drugs such as nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors and integrase inhibitors.

sections.heading: Testing, resistance and stewardship
sections.text: Susceptibility testing guides therapy. Disk diffusion measures inhibition zones; broth dilution gives the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), the lowest concentration stopping visible growth. Resistance mechanisms include drug inactivation (beta-lactamase), target change (MRSA’s mecA gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein), reduced uptake and efflux. Genes spread by plasmids, transposons and integrons through conjugation, transformation and transduction. Stewardship means using antimicrobials only when indicated, with the right drug, dose and duration, guided by culture and local data. Case: Amina’s wound grows a beta-lactamase producer; the team avoids plain penicillin and follows local guidance.

keyPoints: Selective toxicity depends on targets present in microbes but absent or different in host cells.
Beta-lactams and glycopeptides inhibit cell wall synthesis; ribosome, DNA and folate inhibitors act on other bacterial targets.
Antifungals target ergosterol or cell wall beta-glucan; antivirals target viral enzymes such as polymerases, protease or neuraminidase.
Disk diffusion and broth dilution measure susceptibility; MIC is the lowest concentration that stops visible growth.
Resistance can arise by drug inactivation, target change, reduced uptake or efflux, and spread horizontally on plasmids, transposons and integrons.
Stewardship uses antimicrobials only when indicated, with the right drug, dose and duration, guided by culture and local resistance data.

en.title: Diagnostic microbiology
en.short: Specimen collection, culture and identification, serology, molecular tests and report quality.

sections.heading: Specimen collection
sections.text:
A specimen is the material taken from a patient for testing. Collect it from the correct site, at the right time, before antimicrobials when possible, and with aseptic technique to avoid contamination. Use the container and transport medium stated in the laboratory’s instructions. Label the specimen with patient identity and time, and send it promptly; some organisms die if delayed or refrigerated.

Case: a patient with suspected urinary tract infection gives a midstream urine sample in a sterile container. The sample is labelled, kept cool and delivered within the laboratory’s stated time. A delay can raise false positives from contaminating flora. Blood culture bottles should not be refrigerated. National guidance differs, so check local protocols.

sections.heading: Culture and identification
sections.text: Culture means growing organisms on media. A medium supplies nutrients; selective media inhibit unwanted organisms, and differential media show distinguishing reactions. Incubate under stated conditions, then examine colonies and Gram stain. Biochemical identification tests metabolic properties, such as oxidase or sugar fermentation, and commercial kits may help. Results identify a probable organism, not proof of disease.

sections.heading: Serology and molecular
sections.text: Serology detects antigens or antibodies in blood or other fluids. Molecular diagnostics detect nucleic acids, commonly by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or other nucleic acid amplification tests. They can be rapid and sensitive, but contamination causes false positives, and a positive result may reflect past exposure or carriage. Use tests validated for the specimen and syndrome.

sections.heading: Quality and reports
sections.text: Quality assurance covers standard operating procedures, staff training, equipment calibration, internal controls, external proficiency testing and audit. Reports should give specimen type, test, result, units or reference range, interpretation and any limitation. Antimicrobial susceptibility results guide therapy but must be read with the clinical picture. Critical results need urgent communication. Accreditation and reporting rules vary by country.

keyPoints: Collect specimens before antimicrobials when possible, label them correctly and transport them in the stated medium and time.
Culture on selective and differential media, followed by microscopy and biochemical tests, identifies a probable organism.
Serology detects antigen or antibody, while molecular tests detect nucleic acid.
Molecular tests are sensitive but contamination and past exposure can mislead interpretation.
Quality assurance includes standard procedures, controls, proficiency testing and audit.
A report must state the specimen, result, interpretation and limitations, and susceptibility results need clinical correlation.

en.title: Epidemiology and infection control
en.short: Chain of infection, outbreak investigation, healthcare-associated infection and immunisation.

sections.heading: Chain of infection
sections.text:
The chain of infection has six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry and susceptible host. A reservoir is where the agent normally lives and multiplies, such as humans, animals, water or soil.

Transmission may be contact (direct or indirect), droplet, airborne, vector-borne or vehicle-borne, such as food or water. Infection control breaks a link, for example by hand hygiene, safe water, ventilation, vector control or vaccination.

sections.heading: Outbreaks and surveillance
sections.text:
An outbreak is more cases of a disease than expected in a defined place and time. Surveillance is the collection and use of health data; it may be passive, active or sentinel (selected sites).

Investigation starts by confirming the diagnosis and writing a case definition, which states the person, place, time and clinical or laboratory criteria. The team describes cases by time, place and person, forms hypotheses and tests them with comparison studies, while control measures begin early. For example, a ward with several cases of diarrhoea may share a bathroom; cleaning and hand hygiene can stop spread.

sections.heading: Healthcare-associated infection
sections.text:
Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are infections acquired in a healthcare setting that were not present or incubating on admission. Infection prevention and control (IPC) uses standard precautions for all patients: hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, safe injection and sharps practice, cleaning and sterilisation, and safe waste disposal.

Transmission-based precautions add isolation, cohorting (grouping patients) or ventilation for specific routes. Prudent use of antimicrobials and HAI surveillance support these measures.

sections.heading: Immunisation programmes
sections.text:
Immunisation programmes deliver vaccines to individuals and populations. Active immunisation gives a vaccine antigen and produces immune memory; passive immunisation gives ready-made antibody and protects only briefly.

High coverage can produce herd immunity, which reduces transmission to people who are not immune. Schedules, booster doses and target groups differ by country and change over time, so check the current national schedule. Programmes also need a temperature-controlled supply chain (cold chain), safety monitoring for adverse events and surveillance of vaccine-preventable diseases.

keyPoints: The chain of infection has six links: agent, reservoir, exit, transmission, entry and susceptible host.
Reservoirs include humans, animals and environmental sources; transmission can be contact, droplet, airborne, vector-borne or vehicle-borne.
Outbreak investigation uses a case definition, describes cases by time, place and person, tests hypotheses and starts control early.
Surveillance is the collection and use of health data and may be passive, active or sentinel.
Healthcare-associated infections are prevented by standard precautions, transmission-based precautions and prudent antimicrobial use.
Immunisation can be active or passive; high coverage may produce herd immunity, and schedules differ by country and time.

en.title: Food microbiology
en.short: Food spoilage, pathogens, intrinsic and extrinsic factors, preservation, fermentation, safety and laboratory testing.

sections.heading: Spoilage and pathogens
sections.text:
Food spoilage is any change that makes food unfit to eat: off-odours, slime, mould or gas. Microbial growth and enzymes cause it. Spoilage does not always mean danger.

Foodborne pathogens are microbes or their toxins that cause illness, such as Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria monocytogenes, E. coli O157:H7, or toxins of Staphylococcus aureus and Clostridium botulinum. A pathogen may be present with no visible change. Case: rice left overnight at about 30 °C can grow Bacillus cereus; reheating kills cells but not heat-stable toxin.

sections.heading: Intrinsic and extrinsic factors
sections.text:
Intrinsic factors are properties of the food: pH, water activity (aw, available water), nutrients and structure. Most bacteria grow best near pH 7 and need aw above about 0.91; moulds and yeasts tolerate lower pH and lower aw.

Extrinsic factors are the storage environment: temperature, humidity, gases and competing microorganisms. Temperature decides which organisms dominate: psychrotrophs grow in the cold, mesophiles at moderate temperatures, thermophiles when hot.

sections.heading: Preservation and fermentation
sections.text:
Preservation slows or stops growth: chilling, freezing, drying, salting or sugaring (lower aw), acidification, smoking, modified-atmosphere packaging (controlled gas mix), irradiation where permitted, and preservatives. Heat treatment ranges from pasteurisation, which reduces numbers, to canning, which aims to kill pathogens and spoilage organisms. Hurdle technology combines mild methods so organisms cannot overcome all.

Fermentation is controlled microbial growth that produces acids, alcohol or gases and inhibits spoilage: Lactobacillus in yoghurt, Saccharomyces in bread and beer, moulds in soy sauce. Regional examples include ogi, a fermented maize porridge.

sections.heading: Safety and laboratory testing
sections.text:
Food safety management uses HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points): identify hazards, set control points and limits, monitor them and correct failures. Good hygiene and supplier control support it.

Laboratory examination counts total viable organisms and coliforms as hygiene indicators, and tests for specific pathogens by culture or PCR (polymerase chain reaction). Example: 1 mL of a 10^-4 dilution gives 45 colonies, so the count is 45 × 10^4 = 4.5 × 10^5 colony-forming units per mL. Confirm results with official methods.

keyPoints: Spoilage changes food but is not the same as safety; pathogens can be present without visible spoilage.
Intrinsic factors include pH, water activity and nutrients; extrinsic factors include temperature, humidity and gases.
Most bacteria need aw above about 0.91 and pH near neutral; moulds and yeasts tolerate more acidic, drier conditions.
Preservation uses heat, cold, drying, low aw, acid, controlled atmosphere and fermentation, often combined as hurdles.
HACCP identifies hazards and controls them at critical points, supported by good hygiene.
Colony count in CFU/mL or CFU/g = colonies × dilution factor ÷ volume plated.

en.title: Industrial microbiology and biotechnology
en.short: Industrial fermentation, bioreactors, downstream processing, products, strain improvement and quality control.

sections.heading: Fermentation and bioreactors
sections.text: Industrial fermentation uses microorganisms in large, controlled vessels to make a product. A bioreactor is the vessel; it may be a stirred tank or an airlift reactor. Operators control temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, aeration, agitation and sterility. Batch culture adds medium once; fed-batch adds nutrients during the run; continuous culture removes broth and adds fresh medium. Fed-batch is common when high substrate would otherwise inhibit growth or when product forms late.

sections.heading: Products and strain improvement
sections.text: Antibiotics are often secondary metabolites made after growth slows; penicillin from Penicillium is a classic example. Enzymes such as amylases and proteases are often extracellular and made by submerged fermentation. Vaccine antigens are produced under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP); the final product may be inactivated, toxoid, subunit or conjugate, depending on the product. Single-cell protein (SCP) is dried microbial biomass used as protein-rich feed or food; safety depends on the substrate and nucleic acid content. Strain improvement uses mutation and screening, recombinant DNA and metabolic engineering to raise yield, then QC checks that the strain and product are stable.

sections.heading: Downstream processing and QC
sections.text: Downstream processing recovers and purifies the product: harvesting cells by centrifugation or filtration, disrupting cells if needed, extraction, chromatography, crystallisation and drying. Yield and purity are measured at each step. Quality control tests for identity, purity, potency, sterility and endotoxin. Limits and methods come from official pharmacopoeias and national regulators, which vary by country, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: An 800 L broth contains 25 g/L product, so product mass = 25 × 800 = 20,000 g = 20 kg. If 200 kg substrate was consumed, yield = 20 ÷ 200 = 0.10 kg/kg, or 10%.

keyPoints: Industrial fermentation uses controlled microbial cultures in bioreactors to make products.
Batch, fed-batch and continuous modes differ in how medium is supplied and broth is removed.
Downstream processing recovers and purifies the product, and each step affects yield and purity.
Antibiotics are often secondary metabolites, while many industrial enzymes are extracellular.
Strain improvement by mutation, selection and recombinant DNA raises yield but needs quality control.
Product yield = product mass ÷ substrate consumed; here 20 kg ÷ 200 kg = 0.10 kg/kg.

en.title: Environmental microbiology
en.short: Microbes in soil, water and air, element cycles, water quality indicators, bioremediation and waste treatment.

sections.heading: Soil, water and air
sections.text:
Soil is a mixed habitat. Bacteria and fungi live in pore water and on particle surfaces, and the rhizosphere, the zone around plant roots, is especially active. In water most microbes grow in biofilms, communities attached to surfaces.

Air is not a growth habitat. It carries bacteria, fungal spores and viruses on dust and droplets, and their numbers fall with distance from soil and people.

sections.heading: Biogeochemical cycles
sections.text:
Biogeochemical cycles are the routes by which elements move between living things and the environment, and microbes drive them.

In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis fixes carbon dioxide, respiration returns it, and decomposers release carbon from dead matter; methanogens make methane in oxygen-poor places. In the nitrogen cycle, nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas to ammonia, nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrate, and denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas to the air.

sections.heading: Water quality indicators
sections.text:
Faecal pollution is detected with indicator organisms, mainly Escherichia coli and other coliforms. They are abundant in faeces, easy to culture and survive like pathogens, so their presence suggests contamination. The most probable number (MPN) method estimates their density from replicate tubes.

Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) measures organic pollution: the oxygen microbes use over five days at 20 °C. Example: a sample loses 2.0 mg/L dissolved oxygen and a blank loses 0.2 mg/L. With no dilution, BOD = 2.0 − 0.2 = 1.8 mg/L.

sections.heading: Bioremediation and waste
sections.text:
Bioremediation uses microbes to remove pollutants, for example by degrading oil or pesticides. It works best where conditions suit the microbes; adding nutrients is called biostimulation.

In waste treatment, the activated sludge process aerates sewage so microbes oxidise organic matter. Anaerobic digestion turns sludge into biogas, a methane-rich fuel. Drinking-water standards differ by country, so check the current national regulator or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Soil and water are growth habitats; air only carries microbes on dust and droplets.
Microbes drive the carbon and nitrogen cycles through fixation, nitrification, denitrification and decomposition.
E. coli and coliforms are used as indicator organisms for faecal pollution.
BOD is the oxygen used by microbes in five days at 20 °C, corrected by a blank.
Bioremediation degrades pollutants; activated sludge and anaerobic digestion treat waste.
Water quality standards vary by country; check the current official source.

en.title: Agricultural and plant microbiology
en.short: Rhizosphere, mycorrhizae, nitrogen fixation, plant pathogens, biocontrol and soil fertility.

sections.heading: Rhizosphere and mycorrhizae
sections.text: The rhizosphere is the thin soil zone around roots, rich in root exudates (sugars, organic acids) that feed microbes. Mycorrhizae are symbioses between fungi and roots. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) enter root cells and send hyphae into soil, mainly improving phosphorus uptake. Ectomycorrhizae wrap roots in a sheath and are common on trees. The plant supplies carbon; the fungus supplies water and nutrients and can shield against pathogens.

sections.heading: Nitrogen fixation
sections.text:
Nitrogen fixation is the reduction of atmospheric N2 to ammonia by the enzyme nitrogenase. Symbiotic rhizobia form nodules on legume roots; Frankia does the same on actinorhizal plants. Free-living fixers include Azotobacter and some cyanobacteria. Fixed nitrogen enters the soil when roots and nodules decay.

For example, if a legume crop fixes 60 kg N per hectare (a value that varies widely):
60 ÷ 0.46 ≈ 130 kg of urea (46% N).

sections.heading: Plant pathogens and biocontrol
sections.text: Plant pathogens include fungi, bacteria and viruses. Disease depends on a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen and a favourable environment (the disease triangle). Biological control uses living organisms to suppress disease. Mechanisms include competition for space and nutrients, antibiosis, parasitism and induced resistance. Trichoderma species and Bacillus subtilis are studied as biocontrol agents against soil-borne fungi. Biocontrol works best as part of integrated management.

sections.heading: Soil fertility and crops
sections.text: Microbes drive soil fertility: decomposers mineralise organic matter, releasing nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur; mycorrhizae extend root reach; phosphate-solubilising bacteria release bound phosphate. Crop rotation, cover crops and compost support these communities. Case: a smallholder in Ogun State, Nigeria, rotates maize with cowpea. The cowpea fixes nitrogen, and the next maize crop often needs less nitrogen fertiliser. Overuse of soluble fertiliser can reduce mycorrhizal colonisation.

keyPoints: Rhizosphere is the root-influenced soil zone; mycorrhizae improve nutrient uptake, especially phosphorus.
Nitrogen fixation reduces N2 to ammonia by nitrogenase; rhizobia-legume symbiosis is the main agricultural route.
Urea equivalent of fixed nitrogen: kg urea = kg N ÷ 0.46.
Plant disease follows the disease triangle: susceptible host, virulent pathogen and favourable environment.
Biological control works by competition, antibiosis, parasitism or induced resistance.
Microbes build soil fertility through decomposition, nutrient cycling and mycorrhizal associations.

en.title: Research methods in microbiology
en.short: Designing microbiological studies, culture and molecular methods, statistics, ethics and critical reading.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text: Research begins with a clear question and a testable hypothesis. Experimental design sets treatments, controls and measurements before work starts. Controls show what happens without the treatment. Replication means repeating measurements on independent samples, not just re-reading one sample. Randomisation and blocking reduce bias. Sampling must be representative: define the population, choose a method, and collect aseptically. A convenient sample may not represent the site.

sections.heading: Culture and direct methods
sections.text: Culture-dependent methods grow organisms on media. Selective media favour particular groups; colony counts estimate viable cells. They miss organisms that do not grow under the chosen conditions. Culture-independent methods examine the community directly: microscopy, staining, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and sequencing. PCR copies a chosen DNA region; metagenomics sequences DNA from the whole community. These methods avoid growth bias but can be affected by DNA extraction and contamination. Example: 1 mL of a 10^-5 dilution gives 40 colonies, so the original count is 40 × 10^5 = 4.0 × 10^6 colony-forming units (CFU) per mL. Use a countable plate range, often 30 to 300 colonies, and check your protocol.

sections.heading: Molecular and statistical analysis
sections.text: Molecular analysis needs controls: negative controls detect contamination and positive controls confirm the assay works. Statistics turns measurements into evidence. Describe data with the mean and standard deviation, then choose a test that fits the design, such as a t-test for two groups or analysis of variance (ANOVA) for more. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p-values. A p-value is the probability of getting data at least as extreme if the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

sections.heading: Writing, ethics and appraisal
sections.text: Scientific writing follows the IMRaD pattern: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion. Methods must give enough detail for another worker to repeat the study. Ethics covers honesty, plagiarism, data fabrication, authorship, consent and biosafety approval. Critical appraisal asks whether controls, sample size, randomisation and statistics support the conclusions.

keyPoints: A testable question, controls, randomisation and independent replication are the core of experimental design.
Culture-dependent methods count viable cells but miss uncultivable organisms; culture-independent methods use PCR and sequencing.
CFU/mL = (colonies × dilution factor) ÷ volume plated in mL.
Molecular assays need negative and positive controls; statistics should report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p-values.
Scientific writing uses IMRaD; ethics requires honesty, consent, biosafety approval and correct authorship.
Critical appraisal checks whether the design, controls and analysis support the conclusions.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and biosafety
en.short: Professional conduct, laboratory quality and accreditation, biosafety, biosecurity and ethics in microbiology.

sections.heading: Professional conduct
sections.text:
Professional conduct is the set of duties that follow from being trusted with other people’s samples, data and safety. It includes working within your competence, following standard operating procedures (SOPs), recording what was done, reporting errors and near misses promptly, and declaring conflicts of interest.

A microbiologist who cannot perform a method should say so and seek training, not improvise on a clinical sample. Professional bodies publish codes of conduct; the details differ by country and profession, so check the current local code.

sections.heading: Quality and accreditation
sections.text:
Laboratory quality means consistently producing reliable results. It rests on a quality management system: documented methods, trained staff, calibrated equipment, controlled reagents, internal quality control and participation in external quality assessment (proficiency testing).

Accreditation is independent confirmation that a laboratory meets a recognised standard. Medical laboratories are assessed against ISO 15189; testing laboratories against ISO/IEC 17025.
