Accreditation is not the same as certification (for example, ISO 9001 for a management system), and the required standard and national regulator vary, so check current local requirements.

sections.heading: Biosafety and biosecurity
sections.text:
Biosafety protects workers, the community and the environment from accidental exposure. Laboratories are classified into biosafety levels (BSL1 to BSL4), with practices, equipment and facility design matched to the risk. Biosecurity protects dangerous biological materials from loss, theft, misuse or deliberate release. It includes access control and inventory records.

Case: a student finds a culture plate left unattended. The correct response is not to open it but to tell the supervisor and follow the local spill and incident procedure.

sections.heading: Ethics and integrity
sections.text:
Data integrity means records are accurate, complete, legible, contemporaneous (recorded at the time) and attributable. Do not backdate, copy or delete results. Clinical confidentiality means patient information is shared only with those who need it for care or lawful public health action.

Dual-use research of concern (DURC) is legitimate research that could be misused to cause harm. Researchers should seek ethics and biosafety review before experiments that may increase transmissibility or resistance. National rules on consent, data protection and DURC vary; check the current local requirements.

keyPoints: Professional conduct requires competence, honesty, SOP adherence, prompt error reporting and declared conflicts.
Laboratory quality depends on documented methods, training, calibration, quality control and external quality assessment.
Accreditation is independent recognition against a standard such as ISO 15189 for medical laboratories or ISO/IEC 17025 for testing laboratories.
Biosafety controls accidental exposure; biosecurity controls loss, theft, misuse or deliberate release of biological materials.
Data integrity means records are accurate, complete, legible, contemporaneous (recorded at the time) and attributable; clinical confidentiality limits patient data sharing.
Dual-use research of concern needs ethics and biosafety review, and national rules vary so check current local requirements.

en.title: Advanced microbial genomics and bioinformatics
en.short: Whole-genome sequencing, assembly and annotation, comparative and functional genomics, and metagenomics.

sections.heading: Sequencing and assembly
sections.text: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) reads the DNA of one isolate. Short-read platforms give many accurate reads of about 100 to 300 base pairs (bp); long-read platforms give fewer, longer reads that help across repeats. Assembly joins overlapping reads into contigs (continuous sequences) and then scaffolds (contigs ordered with gaps). Short reads are usually assembled with a de Bruijn graph, long reads with overlap methods. Coverage is C = (N × L) ÷ G, where N is the number of reads, L the read length and G the genome size. For N = 1,000,000 reads, L = 150 bp and G = 5,000,000 bp, C = (1,000,000 × 150) ÷ 5,000,000 = 30×. Annotation predicts genes, rRNA and tRNA, then assigns function by similarity to databases; proteins with no match are called hypothetical.

sections.heading: Comparative and functional genomics
sections.text: Comparative genomics compares two or more genomes. Orthologues are genes in different organisms that descend from one ancestral gene through speciation; duplicated copies are paralogues. The pangenome is the full set of genes in a species, divided into a core genome present in all strains and an accessory genome present in some. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms, insertions and deletions, and gene gain or loss reveal relationships and adaptations. Functional genomics asks what genes do. Transcriptomics (RNA sequencing) measures gene expression, and mutant or knockout libraries test gene function by disrupting genes and observing the effect. A gene found in every strain is a candidate core function; a variable gene may be niche-specific.

sections.heading: Metagenomics and community analysis
sections.text: Metagenomics sequences DNA directly from a microbial community, avoiding culture. Amplicon metagenomics amplifies a marker gene such as 16S rRNA for bacteria; it profiles taxonomy but not full gene content. Shotgun metagenomics sequences all DNA and can give taxonomic and functional profiles. Analysis starts with quality control, then classification against reference databases, assembly, and binning into metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Binning uses sequence composition and coverage. Limits include low-abundance organisms, reference bias, contamination and poor strain resolution. Results are hypotheses until checked.

keyPoints: Whole-genome sequencing reads an isolate’s DNA; assembly joins reads into contigs and scaffolds.
Coverage C = (N × L) ÷ G; 1,000,000 reads of 150 bp over a 5,000,000 bp genome give 30×.
Annotation predicts genes and assigns function by similarity; unmatched proteins remain hypothetical.
Comparative genomics uses orthologues, pangenomes, single-nucleotide polymorphisms and indels to compare genomes.
Functional genomics links genes to roles through expression studies and mutant or knockout libraries.
Metagenomics profiles communities; shotgun data can be assembled and binned into MAGs, but abundance and reference bias limit inference.

en.title: Advanced host-pathogen interactions
en.short: Molecular colonisation, immune evasion, persistence, virulence control and model systems.

sections.heading: Colonisation and invasion
sections.text:
Colonisation is the stable attachment and growth of a pathogen on a host surface. Adhesins are surface molecules that bind specific host receptors, often glycans; pili and fimbriae present adhesins at the tip.

Capsules and secreted enzymes help evade clearance. Type III secretion systems inject effector proteins into host cells, remodelling the cytoskeleton and blocking phagocytosis. Tissue tropism follows from which receptors and nutrients are available.

sections.heading: Immune evasion and persistence
sections.text:
Pathogens evade immunity by masking antigens with capsules, varying surface molecules (antigenic variation), switching gene expression on and off (phase variation), and surviving inside phagocytes. Biofilms create a protected community. Persistence may be latent, as in herpesviruses, or a carrier state, as with Salmonella Typhi in the gallbladder.

Host innate sensors such as Toll-like receptors detect conserved molecules and trigger cytokines; inflammation can both clear and feed the pathogen. A teaching case: Amina in Kano, Nigeria has recurrent Helicobacter pylori gastritis; urease neutralises acid, adhesins bind gastric cells, and phase variation of surface molecules aids persistence.

sections.heading: Virulence regulation and host response
sections.text:
Virulence is controlled by two-component systems that sense pH, iron, temperature or osmolarity, and by quorum sensing, which coordinates gene expression as bacterial density rises. Virulence genes often sit on pathogenicity islands and are activated mainly in the host.

The host responds through innate receptors, inflammasomes (innate signalling complexes) and adaptive lymphocytes. The outcome depends on pathogen load, host genetics and immune status, so the same organism can cause mild or severe disease.

sections.heading: Model systems and questions
sections.text:
Model systems include cell lines, organoids (three-dimensional tissue cultures), organ-on-chip devices, and animal models such as mice and zebrafish. Each simplifies the host; findings must be checked in human studies.

Current questions include pathogen heterogeneity and persister cells (drug-tolerant survivors), the role of the microbiome (resident microbial community), trained immunity (innate immune memory), and CRISPR screens (gene knockout screens) for host factors. A key question is why some infections persist despite effective immunity.

keyPoints: Adhesins, pili and secretion systems mediate specific colonisation and host cell manipulation.
Capsules, antigenic and phase variation, intracellular survival and biofilms support immune evasion and persistence.
Two-component systems and quorum sensing regulate virulence in response to host and density cues.
Host innate and adaptive responses determine the outcome; inflammation can be protective or damaging.
Organoids, organ-on-chip and animal models each simplify the host, so human data remain essential.
Current research focuses on pathogen heterogeneity, persister cells, the microbiome and host-directed therapies.

en.title: Microbial biotechnology and metabolic engineering
en.short: Strain design, omics and flux analysis, microbial products, scale-up and regulation.

sections.heading: Strain design
sections.text: Metabolic engineering is the directed change of a microbe’s metabolism, usually by deleting, adding or tuning genes, so that it makes more product or less by-product. Synthetic biology supplies standard DNA parts, promoters, circuits and pathways. Strain design follows a design-build-test-learn cycle: choose a host, block competing routes, express enzymes, balance cofactors such as NADPH, and relieve feedback inhibition. The aim is a robust strain, not only a high titre in one flask.

sections.heading: Omics and flux
sections.text:
Omics and flux analysis test the design. Genomics shows the blueprint; transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics show active genes, enzymes and metabolites. Metabolic flux analysis (MFA) estimates real pathway rates from isotopic labelling and measured metabolites. Flux balance analysis (FBA) uses a genome-scale stoichiometric model and constraints, such as glucose uptake, to predict fluxes under an objective, often maximum growth or product.

Example: glucose to ethanol is C6H12O6 → 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2. Mass yield = (2 × 46.07) ÷ 180.16 = 0.511 g ethanol per g glucose. At 10 mmol glucose gDW−1 h−1, the maximum is 20 mmol ethanol gDW−1 h−1. Real strains fall below this because ATP, redox and growth demands compete.

sections.heading: Products and scale-up
sections.text: Products include biofuels such as ethanol and butanol, bulk chemicals such as lactic and succinic acid, and pharmaceuticals such as insulin and artemisinin precursors. Scale-up moves from flasks to stirred bioreactors. Oxygen transfer, heat removal, mixing, foaming and contamination become limiting, and gradients form in large tanks. A strain that works in a small vessel may fail at scale, so process and strain are developed together.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.text: Regulation depends on product and country. Medicines need clinical trials and approval by bodies such as the US Food and Drug Administration, the European Medicines Agency or Nigeria’s NAFDAC. Genetically modified organisms in food, feed or the environment face separate rules that vary by country. Good practice includes containment, waste treatment and transparent risk assessment. Check the current national regulator before commercial use.

keyPoints: Metabolic engineering changes microbial metabolism by deleting, adding or tuning genes to raise product yield.
Synthetic biology builds standard parts, circuits and pathways, and strain design follows a design-build-test-learn cycle.
MFA estimates real fluxes from isotopic labelling; FBA predicts fluxes from a stoichiometric model and constraints.
Glucose to ethanol has a maximum mass yield of (2 × 46.07) ÷ 180.16 = 0.511 g/g, or 2 mol ethanol per mol glucose.
Scale-up must manage oxygen transfer, heat, mixing and contamination, which change with bioreactor size.
Regulatory approval varies by country and product; check the current national regulator.

en.title: Research project and dissertation in microbiology
en.short: Research question to proposal, design, data analysis, thesis writing, ethics and the viva.

sections.heading: Question and proposal
sections.text:
A research question states what is not yet known. A good one is specific, answerable with the time and equipment you have, and not already settled. A common checklist is FINER: Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant.

The proposal turns the question into a plan: background, aims, methods, analysis plan, ethics, timeline and budget. Write the analysis plan before collecting data, so tests cannot be chosen to fit the results.

sections.heading: Literature review and design
sections.text:
The literature review is a structured search, not a pile of summaries. Record your search terms, databases and inclusion rules so the search can be repeated. Read primary papers, note where they disagree, and state the gap your project fills.

Design follows the question. Experimental work needs controls, replication and, where possible, randomisation and blinding. Computational work needs a written pipeline and versioned databases. A pilot study tests the methods first.

sections.heading: Data, analysis, writing
sections.text:
Keep a data management plan: unique identifiers, a codebook defining every variable, backups in two places, and raw data kept unchanged. Match the statistical test to your design and data.

Case: Amina, an MSc student in Kano, compares two culture methods for Salmonella in street food. She codes each sample, plates both methods in duplicate and keeps a codebook, so replicate agreement is known before comparing methods.

A thesis usually runs: abstract, introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion, references.

sections.heading: Supervision, ethics, examination
sections.text:
Meet your supervisor regularly with written progress, agree deadlines early, and settle authorship in writing. Ethics approval comes before work with human participants, animals or personal data; rules differ by country, so check your institution’s research ethics committee. Pathogen work may also need biosafety approval.

Examination varies. In Nigeria and the UK, for example, a master’s thesis is usually read by an internal and an external examiner, often followed by an oral defence (viva). Check departmental regulations for format, length and deadlines.

keyPoints: A research question should be specific, feasible and answerable with your resources; FINER is a common checklist.
Write the analysis plan before collecting data, so the tests cannot be chosen to fit the results.
Experimental designs need controls, replication and, where possible, randomisation and blinding; computational designs need a documented, versioned pipeline.
Keep unique identifiers, a codebook and two backups, and never edit the raw data file.
Ethics approval must come before any work with human participants, animals or personal data, and requirements differ by country and institution.
In many countries a master’s thesis is examined by an internal and an external examiner, often with an oral defence (viva); check your department’s regulations.
